topics.title: Manipur Government
bullets: After nearly a year under President’s Rule in Manipur, Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand won the floor test by voice vote.
During a special session of the 12th Legislative Assembly, members gave resounding approval to the Chief Minister, signalling the formal restoration of popular government in the state.
Speaker Thokchom Satyabrata then put the Motion of Confidence to a vote, which was approved by voice vote, and adjourned the House sine die. The Manipur Crisis –
The hilly north-east Indian state sits east of Bangladesh and borders Myanmar. It is home to an estimated 3.3 million people.
There are 16 districts in Manipur, but the state is commonly thought of as divided into ‘valley’ and ‘hill’ districts.

In these hill areas, which comprise the bulk of Manipur’s geographical area, live 15 Naga tribes and the Chin-Kuki-Mizo- Zomi group, which includes the Kuki, Thadou, Hmar, Paite, Vaiphei and Zou peoples.
More than half are Meiteis, while around 43% are Kukis and Nagas, the predominant minority tribes.
The Meiteis are the largest community in Manipur. There are 34 recognized tribes, which are broadly classified as ‘Any Kuki Tribes’ and ‘Any Naga Tribes’.
The current churn in Manipur has its roots in the outbreak of ethnic violence between Meiteis and Kuki-Zo groups in May 2023.

What began as clashes quickly hardened into geographic and political separation: Meiteis concentrated in the Valley, Kukis in the Hills, with large-scale displacement, relief camps, and deep mistrust.
Violence began when Kukis protested Meitei demands for official tribal status, fearing it would increase Meitei influence over land and resources in Kuki areas.

Ethnic tensions between the hill communities and the Meiteis have existed from the time of the erstwhile kingdom, but the friction started escalating with the advent of the Naga national movement in the 1950s, and the call for an independent Naga nation.
The Naga insurgency was countered by the rise of insurgent groups among the Meiteis and Kuki-Zomi.

In the 1990s, as the NSCN-IM pushed harder for self- determination, the Kuki-Zomi groups began to militarise, and the Kukis launched their own movement for ‘Kukiland’ — unlike the Naga movement, however, the Kuki-Zomi demand was for a state within India, not a separate national homeland.
Even though the Kukis had started out as protectors of the Meitei people, the Kukiland demand created a rift between the communities.
During the Naga-Kuki clashes of 1993, NSCN-IM cadres allegedly went from village to village in areas they claimed as belonging to Nagas, emptying them of Kuki residents.
Many Kukis fled to Churachandpur, a district dominated by the Kuki-Zomi people.

The Naga and Kuki movements fuelled Meitei nationalism, and numerous groups sprung up in the valley. There were some demands for Scheduled Tribe status for Meiteis, but the discourse remained largely muted.
There has been an organised push in support of this demand for at least since 2012, led by the Scheduled Tribes Demand Committee of Manipur (STDCM).
The 2023 plea before the Manipur High Court was by the Meetei (Meitei) Tribe Union, seeking directions to the Manipur government to submit a recommendation to the Union Ministry for Tribal Affairs.
The recommendation was for the inclusion of the Meetei/Meitei community in the list of Scheduled Tribes in the Indian Constitution, as a “tribe among tribes in Manipur”.

In their plea before the High Court, the petitioners argued that the Meitei community was recognised as a tribe before the merger of the princely state of Manipur with the Union of India in 1949, and that it lost its identity as a tribe after the merger.
It was argued in court that the demand for ST status arose from the need to “preserve” the community, and “and save the ancestral land, tradition, culture and language” of the Meiteis.
Their population which was 59% of the total population of Manipur in 1951 has now been reduced to 44% as per 2011 Census data.
The court directed the government to submit its recommendation after considering the case of the petitioners, “preferably within a period of four weeks” of receipt of the order.
The demand for ST status for the Meitei community has long been opposed by the state’s tribal groups.

One of the reasons cited for the opposition is the dominance of the Meiteis, both in population and in political representation, since 40 out of 60 Assembly constituencies of the state during the time are in the valley.
On May 3 2023, Kuki and Naga tribes protested the potential extension of Scheduled Tribe benefits to Meiteis, fearing it would dilute their affirmative action quotas.
The Kuki-Zo and the Meitei people have stayed apart since, unable to go into each other’s areas.

The violence left more than 250 people dead and some 60,000 others displaced. Following the violent bloodshed that remained volatile for months, the then CM N. Biren Singh came under harsh criticism, accused of failing to restore peace.
On February 9, 2025, after 20 months of prolonged unrest and growing political instability, Mr. Singh resigned due to the threat of a no-confidence motion in a Manipur Legislative Assembly session.
In the 60-member Manipur Legislative Assembly, there are 37 BJP MLAs, which includes seven Kuki-Zo legislators from the party.
In total, there are 10 Kuki-Zo members in the Assembly. The current Manipur Assembly was elected in 2022 and it’s five-year term runs until 2027. The President Rule –
President’s Rule was imposed in February itself after the Union government failed to find a replacement for former CM N. Biren Singh.
Manipur has been placed under President’s Rule for the 11th time since 1951 due to political instability and failure to form a new government.
The last time President’s Rule was imposed in Manipur was from June 2, 2001, to March 6, 2002, lasting 277 days. Article 356 –
Article 356 of the Constitution of India is based on Section 93 of the Government of India Act, 1935.
According to Article 356, President’s Rule can be imposed on any state of India on the grounds of the failure of the constitutional machinery.

This is of two types: ➢If the President receives a report from the state’s Governor or otherwise is convinced or satisfied that the state’s situation is such that the state government cannot carry on the governance according to the provisions of the Constitution. ➢President’s Rule can be imposed if any state fails to comply with all directions given by the Union on matters it is empowered to.
In simple words, President’s Rule is when the state government is suspended and the central government directly administers the state through the office of the governor (centrally appointed).
Parliamentary approval is mandatory for the imposition of President’s Rule, and it must be approved in both Houses of Parliament within two months by a simple majority.
President’s Rule is initially imposed for six months, but it can be extended up to a maximum of three years, with parliamentary approval every six months.
The 44th Constitutional Amendment (1978) introduced limitations on extending President’s Rule beyond one year, preventing its misuse.

President’s Rule cannot be extended beyond one year unless one of the following conditions is met: ➢A National Emergency is in force in India under Article 352. ➢The Election Commission of India certifies that elections cannot be conducted in the state due to difficulties.
After President’s Rule is imposed, the Governor takes over the administration of the state on behalf of the President and is assisted by the Chief Secretary and other appointed advisors.
During President’s Rule, the Governor governs the state directly, making executive decisions without consulting the state council of ministers, as it is suspended.
All financial powers of the state also come under the Union government, and the state budget is passed by Parliament instead of the state legislature.
If the situation improves before the completion of six months, President’s Rule can be revoked at any time by the President on the recommendation of the Union Cabinet. What is a floor test?
A floor test (also called a ‘trust vote’) is held in legislative bodies, to find out whether the government that is suspected to have lost the majority still retains the confidence of the House.
This is done through a vote among the members. When the House is in session, it is the Speaker who can call for a floor test.
But when the Assembly is not in session, the Governor’s residuary powers under Article 163 allow him to call for a floor test.
In case the majority held by the government is questioned, the leader of the party claiming to have the majority has to move a vote of confidence.
They must prove a majority among those present and voting.
The CM moves a motion seeking a vote of confidence, on which MLAs who are present in the House vote.
If the majority of members vote in favour, the government survives; if the CM loses the vote, the government has to resign.
This happens both in Parliament and the state Legislative Assemblies.

Voting can be conducted by either a voice vote, in which MLAs respond to the motion verbally. Voting electronically involves the casting of votes by pressing a button, after which the numbers for each side are displayed on a board.

topics.title: Kunal Kamra Petition
bullets: On February 06, 2026 Kunal Kamra and Sr. Advocate Haresh Jagtiani has filed a petition in Bombay High Court. A division bench of the High Court shall hear the matter on March 16.
The petition has challenged the Sahyog Portal – a tool employed by the central government for online censorship.
The petition also challenged amendment to the Information Technology (IT) Rules that requires social media or online intermediaries to remove such content within 36 hours. What is Sahyog Portal -

The Ministry of Home Affairs’ Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre created this portal to automate the process of sending content takedown requests under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (‘IT Act’).
It brings all platforms/intermediaries (like X) and all authorised agencies (like police) on one platform to ensure immediate action against unlawful content.
The platform is used to remove or disable access to any information or data or link which are used to commit unlawful act. What is Sahyog Portal -
94+ intermediaries have been onboarded onto the Sahyog portal.
This list includes major communication and social media services, such as WhatsApp, Facebook, Instagram, Google, Telegram, Snapchat etc.

The government has also onboarded several e-commerce platforms onto Sahyog, including the likes of Nykaa, Zomato, Blinkit, Flipkart, Amazon, Urban Company, Shiprocket, Reliance Retail, OLX India, Meesho, and IndiaMart. What is Sahyog Portal -
The government will also use the Sahyog portal as the coordination layer for sharing hash data for the non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) hash bank.
This is a system designed to help platforms identify and remove intimate images posted and reshared without consent by assigning “hashes.” Hashes are unique digital fingerprints to images.
However, the development timeline and privacy measures remain unspecified for the bank. How does it work -
Nodal officers of an authorised agency issue notices to platforms through the portal.
Once the platform receives the notice, it will respond to the notices and inform the agency about the action it took.
Platforms can remove content based on the notice or seek additional information. How does it work -
Platforms can also raise a request for non-compliance with a takedown notice citing appropriate reasons.

If the authorised agency agrees with the reasons, then the request will be closed. If the agency that issued the notice does not agree with the reasons for non-compliance, it can further record its reasons for issuing the notice and request compliance.

At this stage, if the intermediary agrees with the reasons behind the notice, the request gets closed. However, if the intermediary still does not comply with the takedown notice, the authorised agency can issue a show cause notice to the platform. How does it work -
If the intermediary responds, it is up to the authorised agency to either accept or reject the explanation.
If the agency rejects the explanation, it can take action against the platform under Rule 7 of the IT Rules (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code), 2021.
This rule says that if an intermediary fails to comply with IT Rules, it will lose safe harbour protection under Section 79. Relevant Laws –

Section 69A of the IT Act: Gives power to the central government to block access to the online content to public under such circumstances which affects the national security, public order and sovereignty of the country.
Section 79 of the IT Act: Protects platforms from liability for the content that a third party posts on their service.
Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act: Platforms can lose this liability if they fail to remove unlawful content after the Government or its agencies notify it about said content. Relevant Laws –
IT Rule 3(1)(d):
Before Amendment: The pre-amendment version of Rule 3(1)(d) authorised any department or agency of the Union or State Government to issue content takedown orders to intermediaries.

After Amendment in 2025: This amendment narrows the category of officers empowered to issue takedown orders, mandates disclosure of reasons for issuing such orders, and institutes a monthly review of issued takedown orders in order to ensure that regulatory intervention is proportionate and compliant with legal standards. Why this petition?

The petition alleges that the automated content takedown mechanism deployed through the Sahyog Portal, operated by various government officials without prior notice to content creators, violates the Supreme Court’s (SC) “necessary safeguards that ensure the constitutionality.”

A Parallel Blocking Regime: The petition argues that the Sahyog Portal creates an arbitrary parallel regime to Section 69A of the IT Act and the IT Blocking Rules, bypassing mandated safeguards and takedown procedures under the IT Act. Why this petition?
It also says this violates principles of natural justice and officials have been unlawfully given the unchecked power to issue takedown and content-blocking orders.

It says IT Rule 3(1)(d) is a “flagrant violation” of freedom of speech and expression, making all content on the internet vulnerable to arbitrary takedowns without providing any remedies to the users.

It also states that IT Rule 3(1)(d) doesn’t fall under the “reasonable restrictions” on fundamental freedom of speech & expression and on the fundamental right to profession and business. Why this petition?

Against Freedom of Speech: It says IT Rule 3(1)(d) is a “flagrant violation” of freedom of speech and expression, making all content on the internet vulnerable to arbitrary takedowns without providing any remedies to the users.

It also states that IT Rule 3(1)(d) doesn’t fall under the “reasonable restrictions” on fundamental freedom of speech & expression and on the fundamental right to profession and business. Why this petition –

The state can’t Issue Blocking Orders under the Union List: It states that blocking orders can’t be delegated to state governments or departments under the Union List of the Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution.

The petition claims that the IT Rule 3(1)(d) is against the landmark judgement in Shreya Singhal’s case that struck down Section 66A of the IT Act that penalised online “offensive messages.” Previously on Sahyog Portal:
In April 2025, X (formerly Twitter) filed a case in the Karnataka High Court against the Sahyog Portal, seeking similar relief regarding Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act.
However, the court dismissed X’s petition in September 2025. X appealed this judgment in December 2025, and the case remains pending.
Delhi HC, in a recent February 2026 order, said it can’t grant safe harbour exemptions to X, if it refuses to onboard the Sahyog portal.

topics.title: Two New Telescope
bullets: In the 2026 Union Budget, two new global telescopes has been approved in order to expand the observational astronomy along with the upgrade of existing global telescope in Ladakh. It is to study the sun and origins of the universe.

The telescopes are named as: (1) National Large Solar Telescope (NLST); (2) National Large Optical–Near Infrared Telescope (NLOT). The existing global telescope is situated in Ladakh which is named as Himalayan Chandra Telescope.
The Union Budget 2026-27 has earmarked INR 13416.20 crores for Department of Science. About the new Telescopes -
National Large Solar Telescope (NLST):
It will be a 2-metre aperture solar telescope built in Merak near Pangong Tso, Ladakh.
Operates in the visible and near-infrared spectrum to study solar magnetism, solar flares, and space weather.
Solar activity affects Earth’s satellites, communication systems, and space missions. About the new Telescopes -
NLST:
NLST will enhance India’s capability to monitor and forecast space weather, protecting national space assets.

Expected to be operational in 5–6 years. Will become India’s third ground-based solar observatory after Kodaikanal Solar Observatory (established 1899) and the Udaipur Solar Observatory (established 1975).
Will complement data from Aditya-L1, India’s first space- based solar mission. About the new Telescopes -
National Large Optical Near Infrared Telescope (NLOT):
It is planned as a 13.7-metre aperture telescope to be established at Hanle in Ladakh. Operational in a decade.
It will employ a segmented primary mirror made up of 90 hexagonal segments, integrated to function as a single reflective surface.
The site’s high elevation, arid conditions, and consistently clear skies will reduce atmospheric disturbance, ensuring high-resolution observations. About the new Telescopes -
National Large Optical Near Infrared Telescope (NLOT):
The facility will enable cutting-edge studies in:
Detection and analysis of exoplanets;
Processes of stellar formation and evolution;
Investigation of supernova explosions;
Research on the early universe and cosmic origins.

Once completed, it will be counted among the largest optical– infrared telescopes worldwide. India’s involvement in the Thirty Meter Telescope (TMT) programme has strengthened its technical capability in advanced segmented-mirror systems. About the new Telescopes -
National Large Optical Near Infrared Telescope (NLOT):

India has experience in the ongoing construction of the Thirty Meter Telescope (TMT), a major international collaborative project involving India, the US, Canada, China, and Japan that aims to significantly advance our understanding of the universe.

TMT has 494 hexagonal mirror segments across the 30-metre primary mirror. India is playing a major role by designing TMT’s Segment Support Assembly, a critical component which controls the mirror assembly and alignment. About the new Telescopes -
Existing Himalayan Chandra Telescope (HCT):
It is operational for 25 years and is set to be modernised by replacing its 2-metre single mirror with a 3.7-metre segmented primary mirror.
The telescope has made substantial contributions to time- domain (transient) astronomy, particularly in tracking brief and dynamic phenomena such as supernova events.
Post-upgrade, it will conduct observations in the optical and near-infrared bands. About the new Telescopes -
Existing Himalayan Chandra Telescope (HCT):
The enhanced HCT will integrate with global research infrastructure, including:

LIGO-India: An Indo-US collaboration, LIGO-India stands for Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, which will comprise an advanced gravitational-wave observatory in Maharashtra’s Hingoli district. About the new Telescopes -
Square Kilometre Array: The Square Kilometre Array is an international project to build the world’s largest and most sensitive radio telescope across two sites (in Australia and South Africa).
This advancement will significantly boost India’s capabilities in studying gravitational wave counterparts and energetic cosmic transients. About the new Telescopes - Significance of new Telescopes -

Locational Leverage – Situated in Ladakh at a longitudinal position underrepresented in existing observatory networks, NLST and NLOT will provide sky coverage that complements and extends current global capabilities.

Generation of Frontier Data – The two observatories will deliver high- precision, first-hand datasets across solar science, astrophysics, and cosmological research, expanding India’s independent scientific contributions.
India’s role in the Thirty Meter Telescope (TMT) project has strengthened its expertise in large segmented-mirror systems. Significance of Ladakh -
Hanle village hosts the Hanle Dark Sky Reserve, India’s first officially designated dark sky conservation area.

The site is characterised by: Negligible light pollution; High elevation (~4,500 metres above sea level); Dry and atmospherically stable conditions; Predominantly clear skies throughout the year; Optimal Observational Nights.
These factors minimize atmospheric turbulence and enhance observational precision, establishing Ladakh as one of the premier astronomical locations in Asia.
